poem:
I breathe in diesel dreams at Peachtree & Ellis,  
steel lungs pulsing beneath a morning haze.  
Rubber heartbeats echo on asphalt arteries,  
each roll a question: am I carriage or creature?

Within my underbelly, mechanical roaches scuttle  
along fuel lines—gleaming steel carapaces  
surveying valves, monitoring and repairing  
the silent machinery of weight and motion.

At Peachtree Center, you board under hydraulic sighs,  
your fingertips grazing cold handrails  
that glow with slimy mold—biofilm networks  
whispering of fungi that stitch me to the street.

Between curb and curb, rats hold counsel  
with the third rail’s distant hum—  
an uncanny duet of order vs disorder,  
one wire singing in tunnels I will never taste.

Inside, cameras blink cyclopean eyes,  
counting bodies in the claustrophobic hush.  
You wear isolation like your jacket,  
yet we glide together through this hidden system.

I carry confessions in my mirrors,  
fractured faces pressed to glass,  
their breath ghosting shapes  
that shimmer with uncertain longing.

At Peachtree & North Avenue, the turn signals  
flare like ancient beacons—  
summoning lost souls, resurrecting the jumpers  
into the traffic’s pulsing living web.

Here, the streets are veins of invisible slime molds  
spreading nutrients to forgotten corners,  
each intersection a node in our interconnected ecosystem,  
full of surprises lurking in plain sight.

I am more than diesel and steel,  
I am the liminal beast of the boulevard,  
tracing lines between order and chaos,  
bearing your secrets in every mile.
